item.title: Higher for Longer Makes High-Quality Credit More Attractive
item.content:encoded:
The Daily Spark

Subscribe View All Sparks Financial Markets & Risk Dynamics

November 20, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

EXPLORE MORE Want More Daily Spark? Daily data-driven analysis on the economy, inflation and capital markets.
  • AI Spending Powers 65% of GDP Growth November 19, 2026
Share

The convergence in yields across asset classes is remarkable, see chart below.

The all-in yield on US investment-grade corporate bonds has moved up to around 6%, now at the top of the range. That is above the S&P 500 forward earnings yield of around 4.5% and above the implied cap rate on all-equity REITs of around 5.7%.

In other words, investors are now paid more to own high-quality credit than to own equities, and with a lot less volatility. The last time IG yields were this far above the S&P 500 earnings yield was in the early 2000s.

Even the 3-month Treasury yield, at around 4%, is now close to the S&P 500 earnings yield. With the AI trade wobbling and the equity risk premium compressed, the case for taking equity risk looks less compelling than it did a few years ago, while all-in yields in high-quality fixed income look increasingly attractive.

item.title: AI Spending Powers 65% of GDP Growth
item.content:encoded:
November 19, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

AI investment added roughly 1.3 percentage points to real GDP growth over the last three quarters, or about 65% of the roughly 2% cumulative growth, led by software and computers, see chart below. These are gross figures that do not net out imports, so the net boost in the national accounts is likely somewhat smaller.

The bottom line is that AI is the number one source of growth for the US economy, and anyone making statements about the 2027 outlook for equity and credit markets is implicitly making assumptions about the pace and magnitude of the AI data center buildout.

item.title: Higher Rates Hit the Fiscal Side, Not the Private Sector
item.content:encoded:
November 16, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Corporate America and households both locked in low rates during the pandemic, with firms refinancing their debt and homeowners securing record-low mortgages.

Washington didn’t, and its interest bill has more than doubled from about $500 billion in summer 2020 to about $1.25 trillion today, so the economy is now far more sensitive to rates through the government than through the private sector, see charts below.

The bottom line is that the cost of higher rates has landed on the fiscal side rather than on companies and consumers, which is why the tightening cycle has done so little to slow the private economy.

item.title: The AI Entrepreneurship Boom
item.content:encoded:
November 15, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

AI is making it much easier to start a business. Entrepreneurial activity continues to rise across all age groups, and AI adopters expect to see faster employment growth than non-adopters, see charts below.

The bottom line is that AI is making the economy more dynamic, and the job-creating effect of AI is far bigger than the labor displacement effect.

item.title: Strong Growth, Rising Prices and a Fed Behind the Curve
item.content:encoded:
November 14, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

October nonfarm payrolls and CPI were strong, the AI spending boom continues and the Atlanta Fed estimates fourth-quarter GDP growth at 3.5%, significantly above the 2% potential growth rate.

At the same time, regional Fed surveys of prices paid, shifted six months forward, point to a continued strong uptrend in inflation, with PCE inflation moving towards 6%, see chart below.

The bottom line is that strong demand, combined with ongoing supply shocks to imports, labor and energy, raises the risk that the Fed is falling behind the curve and will have to raise rates much more than markets currently expect.

For more discussion, see also our recent Spark here.
